stop_rule_S3_note: Counts broken reviews only: unread chunks, nonliteral quotes, wrong identity or schema. Medium confidence is a valid result that fails the ready gate.

r0010.summary: The authors state plainly that their results replicate the original study, and they only note in passing that their effect was significant in the right hemisphere rather than both. They say they cannot conclude much about that difference, so the row should stay successful rather than change to mixed.

r0051.summary: The authors say outright that they replicated the main findings of Vas et al., and they describe the one visible difference, on hyperactivity/impulsivity correlates, as complementing earlier work rather than conflicting with it. The database's current 'successful' should stay, and the change to 'mixed' is not supported.

r0065.summary: The authors formally judge their replication a success and open the Discussion by saying they successfully replicated the most important findings, so changing this row to failed is wrong and the frozen value of successful should stand. They do name a few results that did not replicate, but these are exceptions within a success verdict.

r0077.summary: The authors say plainly that they failed to replicate the main result, the brain response to articles. The noun effect did replicate, but they treat it only as a check that the experiment worked, so failed fits better than mixed.

r0103.summary: The authors repeated their 2018 climate-message experiment and did not find the main effects of the threat and humor messages again, but they say they did replicate the finding that humor only worked for the youngest adults. Because they report one part failing and another part replicating, and give no overall verdict of failure, mixed fits better than failed.

r0146.summary: The proposed change to failed is contradicted by the row it relies on: the overview's coders scored this replication 0.75 and 1, and settled on 1, the top of their 0-to-1 replication scale, with the effect in the same direction as the original. The frozen value of successful should stay, and the replacement quote supports successful rather than the proposed failed.

row:1678.summary: The replication team says in its own words that it only partly replicated the original: no switching delay when results were analysed by participant, but a delay when analysed by item. Mixed fits that statement better than successful.

row:512.summary: The authors, two of whom wrote the original study, say better test scores overturn its claim that inequality grows substantially after school starts, but that part of its summer-versus-school pattern survives. They call this a partial correction, so mixed fits better than failed.

row:2447.summary: The paper says its main aim was to replicate the shift from logarithmic to linear number estimation explored by Booth and Siegler (2006), and it reports doing so for positive numbers. Siegler and Opfer (2003) appears only as background, so Booth and Siegler should replace it and the successful outcome still holds.

row:215.summary: The author's only overall statement is that he replicated Lenski's finding, because status inconsistency had significant effects after accounting for main status effects. He adds that those effects are small next to religion, but never says any part of Lenski's finding failed, so successful fits better than mixed.

row:1308.summary: The authors say their results show both similarities to and differences from Wiklund and Shepherd: two configurations confirm the original and two contradict it, while some hypotheses agree and the universal effect does not. Their doubts about generalizing the finding do not amount to an overall failure, so mixed fits better than failed.

row:1695.summary: The replicators found the same significant interaction as the original but much smaller transfer savings, and they question whether this should count as a true success. That makes mixed better than successful; failed is the closest alternative, but they stop short of saying the replication failed.

row:24.summary: The report says most of the original study's findings replicated, including the main finding, but that its results differed from the original on several parts of Hypothesis 10. That is the authors' own partly-yes, partly-no account, so mixed fits better than successful.

row:2357.summary: The authors call the study a failure to replicate in its title, in their note to the editor and in the conclusion, and they report strong evidence against the critical interaction. A supportive-context speed-up did recur, but they do not treat that as partial success, so failed fits better than mixed.

row:1523.summary: The authors repeated the hands-near-the-screen effect in the one experiment that used only the two original hand positions, but found no effect in three experiments that added more positions. They report both results together, so mixed describes the paper better than successful.

row:869.summary: If this row stays in the database, successful is the right value and mixed is wrong, because the authors call their main test an overall success and never describe it as partial. The open question is whether a study testing a model from its own protocol counts as a replication of that protocol at all, and a person needs to decide that rule.

row:2681.summary: Roodman re-ran Hjort and Poulsen's employment regressions and says his first-row results match theirs exactly or closely, so the numbers were recovered; his much weaker later results come from deliberate revisions, which the unchanged robustness code already captures. The match does not cover every outcome, as Internet usage was re-specified and the World Bank firm data were set aside.

row:1813.summary: The authors say plainly that the Kim and White (2008) effect was not replicated across all 19 schools, so failed fits better than mixed. The programme did look mildly positive in the highest-poverty schools, which the authors call consistent with the earlier studies, but that was an exploratory subgroup, and the earlier studies were run almost entirely in the kind of school where effects here were negative.

row:1345.summary: The report did test robustness: when it re-scored discernment on the original Study 2 data, the link between sharing habit and discernment shrank sharply and the authors doubted it was practically meaningful, so 'not checked' is wrong and 'robustness challenges' fits. This applies to Study 2 only, because the other studies had just a quick review.

row:629.summary: The authors did not find the step-by-step pathway they set out to replicate and favoured continuous over staged development, yet they agreed with the original on attention regulation and on how the systems integrate, so mixed is my preferred value. One opening sentence calls the findings favourable to the original model, and whether that sentence counts as an overall success verdict is a coding-rule decision.

row:2697.summary: The authors say twice that the original conclusions hold up under their alternative analyses, and the coding rules follow their judgement, so robust is supported. Some checks did weaken the result, including no effect for children under 12 months, which is why confidence is medium; the computational reproduction value stays as it is, and the combined outcome would read computationally reproducible, robust.

row:2214.summary: The original found that Polish learners often answered "How are you?" inappropriately; this replication expected the same in Russian learners, but most of their answers were rated as appropriate and the author says her hypothesis was not supported and the results differ significantly from the original. The frozen "successful" appears to confuse the learners' pragmatic success with a successful replication, though the different population, trained raters and lack of a statistical test remain caveats.

row:829.summary: The replication agreed with the original that people with more psychopathic traits and lower self-control were more willing to offend, but the original's 18% figure held only among people with no prior offending (17.5%), against 30.4% in the full sample, which the authors state in their own words. One closing sentence says the study "replicated and extended" the original; I read it as describing what was done rather than a verdict, but a reviewer who treats it as a verdict would keep "successful".

row:1796.summary: The authors say some results differ from the original study (the effect of the speaker's first language did not recur, and treatment preference went the other way) while others match it (better performance and weaker accents were still rated more favourably). That makes mixed a better fit than failed, although the abstract and any conclusion were not in the supplied text.

row:1638.summary: The replication found that people recognised pride above chance, as the original did, but not the original's gender difference, and the author sums this up as a partial replication. Mixed therefore fits better than successful, although the report is inconsistent about which gender scored higher.

row:2678.summary: The author says the original code and data gave back all the numbers in the paper, so computationally reproducible fits better than computational issues. The two coding errors he then found change some estimates when fixed, but they do not mean the published numbers could not be recovered.

row:572.summary: The authors say they replicated their main result, that blood flow in this brain region was higher in people who went back to cocaine. In the same paragraph they say they did not find the link between blood flow and hippocampal size in healthy controls that they had reported before, so 'mixed' fits better than 'successful', although the title and abstract mention only the success.

row:2018.summary: Many Labs 2 found the same effect as Bauer et al., in the same direction and clearly significant, and says the result is consistent with the hypothesis, although the effect was far smaller (d = 0.12 versus 0.87). Nothing in the paper treats part of this test as disagreeing with the original; the main doubt is that so small an effect would not reach significance in samples of ordinary size, which the authors treat as a matter of effect size.

row:2654.summary: The report re-ran the original analysis and obtained the published main result, then argued that a modelling choice about counties with repeat rallies drives it. The numbers reproduced and the conclusion did not hold up, so the computation value should change while the robustness value stays.

row:314.summary: The paper says plainly that it replicates the 2008 magpie study by Prior and colleagues, while Gallup 1970 is cited only as the inventor of the mirror test. The row's failed outcome stays correct for the new original, because the authors say their replication failed to confirm Prior's results.

row:939.summary: The authors say their designated replication closely resembled Jokela and colleagues, finding the same three symptoms linked to CRP. One link fades once extra health and lifestyle factors are added, but they treat that as an extension of the study and not as a disagreement with the original, so successful fits better than mixed.

row:208.summary: The original found that intonation added nothing beyond pauses. This replication found that it did, and the authors say outright that their results differ from the original, so failed is the right label.

row:17.summary: The authors say they replicated four of the original's five significant findings and only part of its regression results, and they reach the opposite conclusion on whether objective and subjective measures agree. Partly replicated, so mixed fits better than successful.

row:1307.summary: Two effects missed significance, including the main pointing effect at p = .06, but the authors judge from the pattern and effect sizes that they replicated the original very closely. Under the rule that the authors' overall verdict decides, this is successful.

row:172.summary: The authors say their results differed significantly from Maurer (2013): the classroom activity did not beat lecture alone, as it had in the original. Attitudes improved in every condition, but that does not preserve the original's comparison, so failed fits better than mixed.

row:1541.summary: The authors tried to repeat three blood-marker findings and say only one, lower CRP in females with substance use disorder, fully replicated, while the IL-8 and IL-10 regression results did not. The CRP-focused title does not make the whole replication a success, so mixed is the better code.

row:2658.summary: The author re-ran the original analysis, recovered its main numbers and concludes that the findings were computationally reproducible, though only from the cleaned analysis data. He also found a coding error and larger p-values on one test, but says these do not change the results qualitatively, so the change is justified with moderate rather than high confidence.

row:2682.summary: The replicators re-ran the original code and data and got every published table back, so the numbers reproduced. They also found a small mistake in the original code, but that is a separate point about the code being wrong, not about the numbers failing to come out.

row:1729.summary: The paper's appendix labels this replication unsuccessful and says nothing else about it, so the source favours failed over the database's successful. One caution: the paper's totals imply one of four such labels may be a mistake, and this could be that one, so checking the project report at osf.io/w9bza would settle it.

row:1675.summary: The replicator says in his own words that he partially replicated the original: one main effect came back and the key training effect did not. That is the database's 'mixed' rather than 'failed', even though the key confirmatory test was not significant.

row:279.summary: The original author's own lab re-ran the study twice and could not recover the original gender-dependent effects. Each study found one different significant result, but the authors attribute these to chance and conclude there is little evidence for the effect, so failed fits better than mixed.

row:2049.summary: This project re-ran 20 scarcity studies and names Chou et al. (2016) as one of only four that replicated successfully, so successful fits this row better than mixed, which describes the project as a whole. The study's own numbers are in a figure and supplement we do not have, so the evidence is the authors' label rather than a visible estimate.

row:2207.summary: The main claim that luxury goods signal a devoted partner did not replicate and slightly reversed, but the assumption that the partner paid for the goods held in both studies. Whether this row is mixed or failed depends on whether that second result counts as agreeing with the original, which only described it; I lean mixed, but this needs a rule decision.

row:2412.summary: The paper says outright that it could not replicate the HDAC9 link with stroke, and its table shows the tested variant was not significant in the large-artery subtype. The partial successes in the paper concern other genes from other original studies, so failed fits this row better than mixed, even though the effect pointed in the same direction.

row:307.summary: The paper is openly a reply to Easterlin's 2005 article and reports that happiness did rise, but its verdict is aimed at the general Easterlin paradox, traced to his earlier papers, and it says it sidesteps the 2005 criticism. Whether this row should point to the 2005 paper, stay on the 1974 chapter or name neither depends on how the closest-study rule applies to replies, and I would not defend the proposed change to the authors without that decision.

row:289.summary: The paper is explicitly an attempt to replicate the host-versus-caller finding in Kroch and Small's 1978 chapter, and it concludes that the finding does not replicate. The database row wrongly points to a book review of the volume containing that chapter, so the correction is right and the failed outcome holds.

row:2463.summary: The paper reproduced the main result of the earlier study, that rare onset cues grab attention against the observer's goal, but it expected and did not find the earlier study's pattern of larger effects after longer gaps between cues, and says so directly. One part agreed and one part differed, so mixed fits better than successful, even though the abstract says briefly that the findings were replicated.

row:2150.summary: The frozen original, a paper on great apes' intuitions about gravity, is not mentioned anywhere in this report, which says one of its aims was to replicate the behavioral findings of Dumontheil et al. (2010) and says it did so. The correction to Dumontheil et al. is right, and the successful outcome holds for that paper.

row:285.summary: This large multi-lab study set out to repeat the 2007 hill experiment and found that infants did not prefer the Helper; the authors say plainly that it did not replicate the original, so failed fits better than mixed. They list method differences that might explain the null result, but they do not say these made the test meaningless, and the verdict applies to the hill task rather than to infant social evaluation in general.

row:948.summary: The authors set out to repeat Morris et al.'s finding in an ordinary classroom course and conclude they could not reliably raise any of the 13 competencies, so failed fits better than mixed. A few competencies did rise, and the failure applies to the classroom version rather than to the original overseas consulting programme.

row:1676.summary: The replication found the same split as the original (similar-sounding distractors hurt free recall but not serial recall), but the key statistical interaction was not significant, and the authors say so as a contrast with the original. They report both agreement and disagreement, so mixed fits better than failed.

row:2269.summary: The paper does check robustness: it swaps Bloom's uncertainty measure for others on the same data and says his results hold, so robust beats not checked. The text supplied is the working paper rather than the published article, so someone must decide whether that version is enough or the published text must be read first.

row:738.summary: The authors say they confirmed most of Rothstein's findings, but they also devote a section to differences: robins did reject eggs differing in only one feature, and the authors dispute Rothstein's conclusion about tuning to cowbird eggs. Because the paper itself reports both agreement and named disagreement, mixed is the right code rather than successful.

row:1932.summary: Many Labs 2 tested this original with two scenario pairs, and in both the difference was significant, in the original direction, and described by the authors as consistent with the double-effect principle. The effects were smaller than the original, but neither test disagreed with it, and a smaller effect alone does not make the result mixed.

row:1285.summary: The report says repeatedly that it replicates the original model from Noor, Brown and Prentice's Northern Ireland paper (2008a); the database's current original, the Chile-related 2008b paper, is only cited once as background. The correction is right, and 'successful' still holds for the new original because the authors say their findings replicate that original test.

row:1626.summary: Only 15 people donated, and the authors say this was too few to interpret the result or draw meaningful conclusions about the original effect. The attempt is better recorded as unable to test the original than as a failed replication.

row:1892.summary: The authors replicated two of the three results they set out to match, including the main effect of the delay, but not the original interaction, and they call the study a partial replication. They add that the main finding held and that the missing interaction was unexpected in the original, but they keep the partial verdict.

row:845.summary: The report replicates a brain-response study of newly learned word meanings by Bakker and colleagues (2015), and its reference list names the Neuropsychologia paper, not the database's paper on brain oscillations by the same authors. The mixed outcome still holds for the corrected original: results at 24 hours matched, but the immediate effect did not appear.

row:106.summary: The authors say two of the three original brain findings came back but the difference between message types did not, and they state that this contrasts with the original study. Mixed fits better than successful, and even the repeated findings relied on a different brain measure from the original's.

row:453.summary: The authors state several times that their ten-lab study only partially confirmed Ulrich et al. (1991): nature improved positive mood and anger more than urban scenes, but fear recovery and sympathetic stress measures showed no nature advantage. Mixed is the right value, and successful overstates what they conclude.

row:2501.summary: The authors say their results support the original's finding that good study design practices were rarely reported, but they explicitly contrast their lack of improvement over time with the original's positive trend. One finding agreeing and one marked as differing makes this mixed, not successful.

row:2651.summary: The authors say they re-ran all the original results with the supplied code and report no mismatch, so nothing in the report supports 'computational issues'. The evidence is mainly that one sentence, and two unexplained sets of 'original' test statistics keep confidence at medium.

row:1871.summary: The report re-ran two of the 2006 paper's studies and found that neither need for cognition nor cognitive load changed how far people adjusted from either kind of anchor, and the authors say they could not replicate the original result. The evidence supports changing the outcome from mixed to failed; a third study also fails, but it tests the separate 2005 paper and is not used for this row beyond the authors' verdict across all three.

row:1329.summary: The report's results agree with both findings it attributes to Yu et al., so successful fits better than mixed. However, the authors worked from the 2018 conference version, while the database row names the later journal article, whose results the report never describes, so someone must decide whether those count as the same original.

row:539.summary: The replication team re-ran three experiments from the same original paper. Two came out matching the original, one did not, and a fourth strand of the work could not be carried out as planned. Because the paper itself reports some agreement and some disagreement and never gives a single overall verdict, mixed fits better than the recorded failed.

row:2505.summary: The replication found the main space-time effect the original reported, but not the original's further claim that the effect grows with the size of the time shift. The authors nevertheless state plainly that their results largely replicate the original and reinforce its conclusion, and that overall judgement is what the coding rules follow, so successful is right.

row:1557.summary: The authors re-ran their 2017 forgiveness study with new participants, got the same pattern with the original questionnaire and with negative thoughts, and state that their model was replicated. The one null result, for positive thoughts, comes from a new measure they treated as an open question, so successful fits better than mixed.

row:881.summary: The authors predicted that Fleeson's finding would replicate, and in two new experiments people enjoyed acting extraverted whatever their personality, as Fleeson found. The mixed results they mention concern a separate new question about Stroop performance after acting out of character, so successful fits better than mixed.

row:448.summary: The original found both models made fewer false alarms than the standard methods. On real data one model still did, but the author says the other did worse, contrary to the original, so mixed is the right code and the general praise for machine learning is not a verdict on the replication.

row:471.summary: The study set out to replicate the scale's factor structure in Black men and says plainly that it did, so successful is right for this original. The scale's failure in White women concerns a group the original never studied, and belongs to the paper's extension.

row:2673.summary: The team re-ran the authors' code and says it reproduced the main findings and virtually all figures and tables, with differences it calls cosmetic. A few supplementary tables would not compile or differed slightly, but the authors do not treat these as undermining the main results, so computationally reproducible fits better than computational issues.

row:129.summary: The authors say their study gives both confirming and contradicting evidence against Ott et al. (2018): multiple representations again helped and gaze switching matched, but text was not the reference representation, which they say contradicts the original. That is the paper's own partly-yes, partly-no framing, so mixed fits better than successful.

row:848.summary: The author says overall, three times, that the studies replicate Baumeister et al. on belief in free will and helping, and the coding rules let that verdict decide. The support is thin: the correlation was significant in two of five studies, belief in dualism predicted helping better, and the original experiment's causal claim was not re-tested.

row:2770.summary: The report gives no overall verdict but says two of the nine claims replicated and seven did not, which the coding rules call mixed. Mixed flatters the result somewhat: every test of the paper's main effects failed, and the two successes rest on lenient criteria.

row:1469.summary: The authors say they supported four of Hsee's five effects and not the fifth, the more is better effect in the dish-set study, which was one of their core predictions. Their title says mostly successful, which also describes a partial result, so mixed fits better than successful.

row:2393.summary: The authors say they could not replicate the headline link between Black residents' share and COVID-19 risk in Phoenix, yet they also say the original's neighbourhood predictors stayed associated and one direct model agreed in direction and range. Mixed fits that two-sided account better than failed, though failed is a serious alternative because the headline finding is the part that did not hold.

row:1351.summary: Re-running the authors' own data and code gave the reported numbers for all six claims. The only flagged miss is a coefficient of 0.8085 against a printed 0.808, which the analyst attributes to rounding, so computational issues overstates the discrepancy.

row:146.summary: The authors say they replicated Volling's activation parenting profile in both parents, but also that the mother-father pattern seems inconsistent with Volling: here mothers, not fathers, more often showed that profile, against their own hypothesis. Mixed captures both, though the authors' upbeat replication language makes successful a serious alternative.

row:657.summary: The authors tried to confirm six gene regions from their earlier scan; one was confirmed, one had weak support and four were not confirmed, so mixed fits better than successful even though the title and conclusion highlight the one confirmed region.

row:2170.summary: The author mainly re-ran Kleck's analysis and got a different main result, so reproduction with computational issues fits. The replacement quote covers robustness: Kleck's finding of no link to total suicides was not recovered and the link reversed with age, though only the computation quote in the supporting list covers the first axis. Applying this must also clear the old failed outcome, and the US replication arm would then no longer be recorded in this row.

row:708.summary: The authors confirm that graphic warnings in ads affect quitting outcomes through fear, as Kees et al. (2010) found, but state that, in contrast to that study, moderate and high graphic warnings had similar effects. They describe the overall pattern as replicating many conclusions alongside these differences, so mixed fits better than successful, though the paper's closing 'confirm and extend' sentence gives successful a real competing case.

row:1484.summary: The German replication did not reproduce the main claim that framing affects men and women in opposite ways, but the authors themselves conclude that their results are partly consistent with the original, citing agreement on no general framing effect and on men giving nothing more often when taking. Failed is the strongest alternative if only the central claim counted, but the authors' own overall wording points to mixed.

row:1679.summary: The replication team targeted one effect, that words with many close neighbours in meaning are judged more slowly, found it in the same direction and called the attempt successful. The effect was about half the original's size and a secondary distant-neighbour effect was not detected, but the report does not present either as a partial failure, so successful fits better than mixed.

row:2504.summary: The authors say plainly that they could not replicate the 6p21.1 association from Holliday et al. (2012), and this was the only tested locus whose effect ran in the opposite direction. The paper's successes concern other loci from other studies, so mixed does not fit this row and failed does, although the authors note their power was limited.

row:1593.summary: The authors' close repeat of the 2002 experiment failed, but they also ran a looser version that partly matched the original, and they sum up the two together as mixed support. Mixed therefore fits the row as a whole, with the caveat that failed remains an accurate description of the close repeat alone.

row:805.summary: The authors say they replicated the original's prediction and partial mediation results, but they found a moderation effect the original did not find and call that a divergent finding. Partly agreeing and partly differing in the authors' own words is mixed, not successful.

row:1921.summary: The replicators say the centroid result replicated but the single-distractor result did not, and that only some results partly replicated, so successful is wrong and mixed fits their own account. A reader could argue for failed, because they also say the original conclusion cannot strictly be drawn and call the single-distractor result crucial.

row:1040.summary: The author reruns the original two choice tasks and gets the same pattern, but his main message is that the pattern comes from people answering at random rather than from a real preference for certainty, which fits 'statistically successful but flawed' rather than 'failed'. The paper does not re-test the Afghan fear and violence effects, so the verdict covers only the certainty pattern.

row:276.summary: The original author and a colleague updated the custody problem's parent descriptions, ran it twice with new samples, got the original pattern both times, and state that this fully replicates the 1993 findings, so 'successful' fits better than 'mixed'. They also accept that the old wording no longer works, so this success applies to the updated materials and does not cancel the failures reported elsewhere.

row:2151.summary: The authors say most of the original's results held, especially that the device rarely changes answers to sensitive questions, but that others did not, such as where people answered and trust in confidentiality. Mixed matches that two-sided conclusion better than successful.

row:294.summary: The paper says in its title and abstract that it tried and failed to replicate the experiment in Boroditsky et al. (2003), and it never mentions the Clark chapter in the frozen row. The original should change to Boroditsky et al., with the failed outcome unchanged and the DOI left blank because the paper prints none for it.

row:1034.summary: The replication again found that sentences affected hand muscle responses early on, which the authors call consistent with the original, but the effect ran in the opposite direction and the behavioral experiment did not replicate. Mixed reflects that partial agreement better than failed, though a reversed effect makes this a closer call than most.

row:2131.summary: The authors say they replicated Aguado's two-way interaction when many different faces were used, but that it failed to replicate when the same four faces were repeated, so mixed fits better than successful. The small-set failure was predicted and marks a limit on the effect rather than an error in the original, which is why confidence is medium.

row:2662.summary: The authors say plainly that the paper's main results reproduce, both with the original code and in their own R version. What remains is software-version trouble and some unexplained differences in appendix tables, which they say do not change the conclusions, so computationally reproducible fits better than computational issues.

row:67.summary: The original found that this variability measure did not fall as learners progressed. This study found that it did fall with proficiency and calls that a stark contrast with the original, so failed fits better than successful, even though the authors welcome the result as support for the underlying theory.

row:2751.summary: The report checks five claims from one paper in newer survey data: the three about economic evaluations were not replicated and the two about security evaluations were. It gives no overall verdict, so mixed fits better than failed, despite one result paragraph that mislabels the security coefficient as economic.

row:2370.summary: The report's authors say they repeated Salmela and Laurinen's 2009 experiment and replicated its main findings, so that study is the right original and successful is the right outcome. The failure in the title refers to computer models of lightness, not to this replication; White (1979) only supplied the illusion, and the outcome change holds only together with the change of original.

row:861.summary: The authors say plainly that their Experiment 1 replicated Chan and McDermott's third experiment: testing improved recollection, not familiarity, compared with studying once. Their later experiments ask a different question about restudying, so successful fits this row better than mixed.

row:2621.summary: The authors say they replicated the main finding that people recognised the words above chance, but could not confirm any of the original's other observations. That is a partial replication in their own words, so mixed fits better than failed, even though their stricter re-analysis casts doubt on how far the main result generalises.

row:677.summary: The authors replicated the part of Jiang and Forster they call most critical, but they say another part did not hold: priming from the first to the second language appeared where the original found none. They state that the experiment did not fully replicate the original, so mixed fits better than successful.

row:2774.summary: The report re-tested 13 claims from Vadillo et al. (2016) on a different dataset: 7 replicated and 6 did not, and the authors conclude that some of the problems Vadillo identified appear but not all claims hold. That is a mixed result rather than a failure.

row:1347.summary: Frozen 'not checked' is wrong: the author refit the original models on the original data and says the estimates and WAIC ordering closely match the original. The match is the author's judgment and is not exact, because printed WAIC values differ by about 1%, a gap larger than the difference between the models, so a stricter reading of 'negligible difference' could give 'computational issues'.

row:2233.summary: The Pakistan study confirms most of what the Indian study predicted, but its authors say one prediction (the boy-girl gap peaking at middle birth order) was not supported and one trend differed from the Indian result. That makes 'mixed' a better label than 'successful', despite the introduction's broad claim of confirming the Indian findings.

row:491.summary: The replication team repeated one experiment from the glioblastoma paper, measuring Tie2 levels in the original study's own cells, and reported that their results pointed the same way as the original and were statistically significant where expected. A second experiment from the same paper was abandoned before producing any result, which is a gap rather than a disagreement, so 'successful' fits the completed comparison better than 'mixed'.

row:1458.summary: The analyst could not run the original analysis because the shared dataset lacked the variables the code needed and there were no instructions for preparing it, so no comparable numbers were produced. That is a technical failure rather than a case of numbers that came out differently.

row:322.summary: Using Sicherman's own approach on German data, the authors got the same result he did, but they argue that his way of measuring career moves and his model are not a valid test of the theory. With a measure they consider better (wage growth), they find the opposite, so the original effect was obtained but judged flawed rather than simply failing to replicate.

row:2009.summary: The authors re-ran the heart-rate part of the angry-faces freezing study and conclude they 'largely replicated' it, so successful follows the rule that an author's overall verdict decides. They also say one anxiety correlation did not replicate and the anxiety effect was weak, and body sway was never measured, so this is a qualified success and mixed is the main rival reading.

row:2166.summary: This paper re-ran Ashraf and Galor's own analyses and recovered their numbers, then showed the findings weaken once a coding error is fixed and specifications or data change, which fits a reproduction that computes correctly but has robustness challenges. The weakest step is the type change, because the authors call it a replication and much of their headline rests on added data, though they collected none themselves and the proposed values hold on the original data alone.

row:261.summary: The report calls itself a conceptual replication using the materials of Pelzl et al. (2019) and compares its results with that paper, whereas Pelzl et al. (2020) is only cited in passing, so the original should change to the 2019 paper. Mixed still holds for that paper: behaviour agrees, but the brain-response difference between tone and rhyme errors appears here and not in 2019.

row:1005.summary: The authors rebuilt the original airline data from the same sources, ran the original code and recovered the main numbers closely, so this is a reproduction whose computation worked. The finding then does not hold up: correcting for market-share endogeneity and several other reasonable changes remove the statistically significant link between common ownership and ticket prices.

row:199.summary: The authors call their study a successful replication of the earlier gene finding, in the abstract and again in the closing sentence, so successful is the right code under the rule that an author's overall verdict decides. The success is for the gene region only: they did not find the earlier association with the specific T allele, and they say so.

row:127.summary: The report's only 2008 Mechling reference is Mechling, Gast and Fields, not the Mechling and Gustafson paper on the frozen row, so the original should change. Against that study the authors report the same immediate gains and maintenance but say the learning pattern differed, which makes the outcome mixed.

row:736.summary: The study set out to repeat two earlier findings about eye gaze. The authors say one held (mutual gaze helped) and the other reversed (longer speaker gaze went with fewer correct responses), so mixed is the right code rather than successful.

row:789.summary: The authors say their distress and brain-response results agree with the original, but they explicitly contrast the timing: their effect appeared early, while the original's appeared late, and the late effect here missed significance (p = .06). They give no overall verdict, so mixed fits better than successful, although their tone is favourable and they offer a possible explanation for the timing difference.

row:238.summary: The authors state outright that their two studies replicate the original findings with smaller effects, which decides the outcome as successful. They also admit they never ran the original's comparison with people playing alone, so that part is untested rather than contradicted.

row:2693.summary: The comment's authors conclude the main findings reproduced and call the problems they found minor, so computationally reproducible fits their verdict. A human reader should note that this covers nine of over 70 models and that some credible intervals differ beyond rounding, one of them enough to cross the no-effect line, though the authors treat these differences as small.

row:971.summary: The authors say plainly that Experiment 1 replicated Ishihara's effect using the same kind of direct timing judgment. The later experiments found no effect, but they used a different task to ask a new question about automatic processing, so they limit where the effect appears and do not undercut the original result.

row:1205.summary: The first study found that protagonist race made little difference to engagement but that children tended to pick books with a protagonist who looked like them, and this replication found the same two things. The 'failed' record seems to treat the lack of an engagement effect as a failure, although that matches the original; the main caveat is that the preference result comes only from White children and the authors never state an overall verdict.

row:432.summary: The authors compare their Japanese results with the original directly: guilt's helpful indirect effect came through, but guilt's harmful direct effect and pride's helpful effects did not. The paper gives no overall verdict, so 'mixed' fits better than 'successful'.

row:580.summary: The authors say their analysis of why alexithymia and emotional intelligence are linked replicates the earlier study, but their finding on what causes differences in alexithymia contrasts with it. Their praise of the replication covers only the first part, so 'mixed' fits better than 'successful'. The agreeing passage sits too far from the contrast to fit in one quote, so it is listed separately.

row:184.summary: Some early experiments found nothing, but the author weighs all of them and concludes that the primacy effect is real, only much smaller than Asch reported. Under the coding rules a smaller effect with a positive overall verdict is 'successful', not 'mixed'.

row:91.summary: The authors say in so many words that Study 2 only partially replicated this paper: the intervention again helped low performers, but the expected route through perceived usefulness did not appear, which they call surprising and contrast with this original. Mixed fits better than successful, even though the abstract says 'replicated' when describing the low-performer effect.

row:250.summary: Individual correlations came out unevenly between the two studies, and the authors say so, including one explicit disagreement with the original in Study 1. But having weighed this, they conclude across both studies that the original associations are reasonably robust and their findings broadly in line with it, so successful fits better than mixed.

row:1231.summary: The authors ticked 'mixed' rather than 'failure' in their own evaluation and describe a partial replication: the overall difference between conditions came back, but the faster-learning-with-labels pattern did not. 'Mixed' is the right code, though the abstract's plain statement that the key result failed should stay visible.

row:468.summary: The change of original looks right: the experiments copy specific Aknin et al. (2013) studies, and the authors say they chose that paradigm over Dunn et al.'s (2008). What remains open is the outcome, because the proposal keeps 'mixed' although the authors' overall conclusion is positive and one experiment failed, so someone needs to decide which of those governs.

row:412.summary: The report replicates the 2014 paper on ADOS domain scores by Hus, Gotham and Lord, not the Module 4 paper currently recorded, which it barely touches. The authors clearly say the original finding was confirmed in a new sample, so 'successful' still holds, with the caveat that the youngest age groups could not be tested.

row:2285.summary: The authors agree with DeBruine et al. that similarity and kinship judgments are closely linked but not the same, yet they say their sex result went against that study and they did not find its accuracy difference, so mixed fits better than successful. The abstract's 'in line with DeBruine' sentence is the main argument for keeping successful, which is why confidence is medium.

row:928.summary: All four new samples failed to find the moderation by greed that Piff et al. reported in Study 7, and the authors treat that interaction as the primary test, so failed fits better than mixed. Confidence is medium because the greed prime did raise unethical behaviour in three samples and the corrigendum text was not available.

row:1635.summary: The replication team says some parts of the original results replicated: the behavioural support effect held, while the priming effect and most other outcomes did not, so mixed fits their own summary better than failed. Confidence is medium because the planned main test came out null and the verdict comes from the project report rather than the Science article named on the row.

row:2391.summary: This is a real replication that failed, and the outcome is not in doubt. The report credits the same anal-organ result to Waddington 1953 in its abstract and verdict sentence but to Waddington 1959 in its detailed account, so 1959 is the better fit but replacing 1953 needs a rule for inconsistent citations or a check of the original papers.

row:1580.summary: The authors say outright that they did not replicate Ert and colleagues' Study 1: trustworthiness did not raise prices and attractiveness did. The successful part of the paper concerns a different original study, so failed is the right outcome for this row, not mixed.

row:1542.summary: The authors say some results match Croninger et al. (school SES and reading; the reading-course average) and others do not (school SES and mathematics; the other teacher characteristics), so mixed fits better than failed. A human should know that the reading-course match is doubtful, because the paper's own table shows that effect as negative while its discussion calls it positive.

row:2685.summary: Re-running the original code gave the original numbers, and the authors say so directly. The leap-year bug they found is an error in the original code that barely moves the results, not a failure to reproduce them, so computationally reproducible is correct for the temperature-mortality results they checked.

row:2660.summary: The frozen row lists the comment's own authors as the original, but the paper states it re-tests Mayshar, Moav and Pascali (2022), so the original should change. The original numbers were obtained again apart from small differences the authors say do not matter, so computationally reproducible is correct for Table 1, and the existing robustness challenges value still holds.

row:1590.summary: The authors state plainly that their direct replication of Ihme and Tausendpfund's Study 2 failed, in both stages and on their preregistered test, and they report evidence that the stereotype effect is absent. They did find that men scored higher than women, but that was not the claim being tested, so the row should read failed rather than mixed.

row:752.summary: The authors say themselves that their South African results show both similarities to and differences from Sirieix et al.: the top two factors match, but other rankings and the preferred strategy differ. They call some differences minor, but they never say the original was simply confirmed, so mixed fits better than successful.

row:2372.summary: The paper says it replicates the 2016 recycling experiment, copies that study's name manipulation, and contrasts its null results with that study, so the 2016 paper is the right original rather than the 2014 policing study it cites as background. The existing failed outcome still holds for the 2016 original, even though the authors stress that the null may reflect the change of policy area.

row:730.summary: The supplied text clearly replicates Wills 2016 and calls the replication successful, but it describes itself as a student-level companion to the class-wide 2018 article that this row names. The row's current original, Kamps 2015, may be right for that class-wide article, so someone needs to check the published version before changing it.

row:452.summary: The authors report that reviewers still favour production code and look at it first, as in the original study, but say that review balance and the topics discussed differ notably on GitHub. They present both agreement and difference, so mixed fits better than successful.

row:2663.summary: The comment's authors got Montero's published worker-income numbers when they reran his data and code, and then showed those numbers do not hold once errors are fixed. Under the coding rules that means the computation reproduced, while the failure belongs under robustness.

row:2772.summary: The report plainly says the replication failed: the two narcissist subgroups the original described could not be found consistently, so the self-esteem comparison was never run. Nothing in it supports the recorded successful outcome.

row:1102.summary: The authors did see resveratrol activate SIRT1 with the same fluorescent test substrate as the original paper, but with no other substrate, and they conclude that the original claim is likely an artifact of that test. That fits an effect that was obtained but comes from a flawed method better than a plain failure to replicate.

row:2684.summary: The authors reran the analysis many ways and conclude the tax effect on output is fairly robust, with most failures coming from setups they consider too short on lags. Some checks do weaken significance, especially on the immediate effect, but their overall conclusion favours robust over robustness challenges.

row:237.summary: The paper clearly set out to repeat the authors' own 2017 study and says it succeeded, so 2017 with successful is well supported. The same paper also says it did not reproduce the 2014 learning benefit, so whether this should replace the 2014 row or sit beside it is a rule decision.

row:505.summary: The authors cite Bickel et al. (2016) among the four studies that reached significance and call those four successful replications. Their broader caution about the field does not make this particular study a failure.

row:759.summary: The paper says outright that it replicates the empathy effect from Hurlemann et al. (2010), and also from two Geng et al. (2018) papers, so the existing row is correct. Geng et al. (2018b) could be added as its own row but should not replace Hurlemann et al. (2010).

row:632.summary: The authors say they found the same four symptom groups and the same links to daily functioning as their 2019 study, but state that the childhood-adversity result was not replicated. One unqualified highlight line sounds like a full success, but the abstract and conclusions show it refers to the symptom groups.

row:537.summary: The replication matched the original on one result: lowering the candidate genes reduced PTEN protein in normal HCT116 cells. It differed on the reporter, overexpression, microRNA-dependence and cell-growth results, and the authors give no overall verdict, so mixed fits better than failed.

row:306.summary: The authors clearly failed to replicate the unconscious thought advantage, but they do not single out one original. They name the 2006 theory article and the 2004 experimental paper together, so the swap to 2004 alone needs a rule on which counts rather than a reading of the text.
